recentItems.title: Partial lunar eclipse visible across the Americas, Africa and Europe
recentItems.description:
Skywatchers across parts of the Americas, Europe and Africa witnessed a partial lunar eclipse from Thursday (August 27) into the early hours of Friday (August 28), as Earth moved between the Sun and Moon and cast its shadow across the partial lunar surface.

In Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, crowds gathered to observe the celestial event, which reached its peak at 4:13 a.m. GMT. Nearly the entire Moon, or 96.3% of it, was covered by Earth's shadow.

Astronomer Alexandre Cherman said the eclipse was not total but was “almost total,” noting that it was the last lunar eclipse of the year.

The phenomenon was also observed in Mexico City, where residents gathered at the Monument to the Revolution to watch the Moon between the clouds.

In Bolivia, sky enthusiasts observed the eclipse from La Paz, where the city's elevation of more than 3,000 meters provided optimal viewing conditions due to reduced atmospheric interference.

Planetarium and Astronomical Observatory director Mirko Raljevic said the color produced by the Moon during the eclipse could provide an indication of the condition of Earth's atmosphere.

The Moon also turned a dusky red over parts of the United States and Canada, including Anaheim and Vancouver.

The eclipse was visible over Senegal and Tunisia in Africa, as well as Athens, Rome and Spain in Europe.

In Tunisia, the partial eclipse covered 93% of the lunar surface at its peak, while in Athens, about 84% of the Moon was obscured at the best visible stage.

In Rome, roughly 93% of the Moon's diameter was immersed in Earth's dark inner shadow, with the eclipse seen above the dome of St. Peter's Basilica.

Spain also witnessed the eclipse throughout its territory, with the Moon appearing red during the totality phase before eventually setting over Madrid. — Report from Reuters

recentItems.title: Rescuers dig for survivors in Nepal as fresh floods loom
recentItems.description:
Rescuers in Nepal continued searching for survivors on Friday (August 28) after devastating flash floods killed at least 489 people, while a newly formed lake along the Nepal-China border began overflowing, forcing authorities to halt rescue operations.

Heavy machinery clawed through mud in Trishuli as rescuers searched for survivors amid damaged buildings and vehicles.

The Nepal Prime Minister's Office also released footage showing rescuers climbing through thick mud toward a tunnel at the Upper Trishuli Hydropower project, where laborers and local residents were trapped by the floods.

Rescuers were seen carrying people covered in mud out of the tunnel and pulling others through the mud to safety.

Meanwhile, Nepal halted rescue work in the flood-hit Trishuli valley after a lake formed by a landslide on the Nepal-China border began to overflow.

Officials in Nepal's Rasuwa district said they received notice that the lake had broken its banks, two days after a flash flood hit the region.

Satellite images showed the barrier lake formed by glacier debris at the border between Nepal and China's Tibet Autonomous Region.

Residents in Nepal's Nuwakot district evacuated to higher ground in Trishuli as authorities warned of a possible surge in river levels. Rescue workers and authorities guided residents away from flood-hit areas, including a woman pushing a man in a wheelchair.

In Nuwakot, families continued searching lists of rescued and missing people while awaiting news of their loved ones.

Meanwhile, China dispatched hundreds of military personnel and rescuers to the border town of Gyirong in Tibet following the collapse of a wall of ice, mud and rock into a mountain river that triggered a catastrophic flash flood.

Australia also announced aid for communities affected by the floods along the Nepal-China border and said it would deploy additional consular staff to the area. The number of missing Australians rose to 39.

For some families and tour operators, the search remained deeply personal. Sunil Shrestha, a tour operator whose drivers and staff went missing, said he sent a pilot to search for their vehicle at its last known GPS location, but found no sign of it.

“At the time I lost my hope,” Shrestha said. — Report from Reuters

(Production: Cooper Inveen, Daniel Lim)

recentItems.description:
